name: Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants (NaSSAs)
summary: The NHS groups antidepressants into types such as SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs, and lists mirtazapine as a noradrenaline and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA). Mirtazapine is the NaSSA covered on this site.
mechanism: Pharmacology reviews describe mirtazapine as blocking alpha-2 receptors on nerve cells in the brain, which increases the release of noradrenaline and serotonin, and as also blocking 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 serotonin receptors. Unlike many other antidepressants, it is described as not inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline or serotonin. Blocking histamine H1 receptors is linked to its sedating effect.
cautions: The NHS says mirtazapine is not usually recommended for anyone under 18.
The NHS says stopping an antidepressant suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and the dose is usually reduced gradually.
The NHS says mirtazapine can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy.

classInteractions.effect: The NHS says it should not be taken during mirtazapine treatment because it increases the risk of side effects.

classWarnings.text: The NHS side effects page says to call 999 or go to A&E now if a person has thoughts of harming themselves or ending their life, while the main NHS mirtazapine page says to call NHS 111. Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123 at any time.
